prompt.context: Our client is an opera house located in a large metropolitan city. They have been struggling with declining profitability recently and have hired McKinsey to help them understand the source of declining profits and provide recommendations on how to turn the situation around. The opera house only does opera performances. It offers 6 unique performances per year, each repeated for a few weeks. The opera house has been around for 50+ years. Customers are typically 45+ years old, highly educated, and come from the suburbs.
prompt.question: Why is the opera house experiencing declining profitability, and what recommendations would you make to turn the situation around?

clarifying_info.q: What are the ticket products and prices?
clarifying_info.a: Single show tickets: Night shows at $100, Sunday matinee at $70. Club member tickets (all 6 shows of the year): Night package at $480, Matinee package at $300. Group discounts (10 or more single shows): Night tickets at $80, Matinee tickets at $60. Night shows are Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Memberships are for a single night (e.g., Wednesday night membership).

clarifying_info.q: What is the traffic / volume by show day?
clarifying_info.a: Thursday nights average 300 customers, Friday nights average 450, Saturday nights average 450, Sunday matinee averages 500. Capacity is 500 seats.

clarifying_info.q: What does the ticket mix look like?
clarifying_info.a: On average regardless of day: single tickets 70%, group tickets 10%, club members 20%.
The client has calculated fixed and variable costs attributed on a per-show basis. They feel good about $30,000 as a proxy for the real cost of running each show.

clarifying_info.q: What are the substitutes for opera?
clarifying_info.a: What do you think the substitutes would be? (Interviewer asks candidate to list at least 4, then says: That sounds about right; unfortunately I do not have any information in this area.)

framework: Revenue analysis: break down by show type (night vs matinee), ticket category (single, group, club), and day of week to identify underperforming segments
Volume/traffic analysis: compare attendance vs capacity across each show day to find capacity utilization gaps
Pricing analysis: assess price points for each ticket category and potential for optimization
Cost structure: separate fixed vs variable costs; understand per-show economics and contribution margin
Profitability by show day: calculate revenue per day, subtract per-show cost, identify loss-making days
Growth levers: evaluate ways to increase traffic, raise average ticket value, or reduce costs

questions.prompt: Calculate the revenue for each show day and identify which days are profitable.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the ticket mix (70% single, 10% group, 20% club) to each day's attendance and the respective night prices, then subtract the $30,000 per-show cost. Thursday should be identified as unprofitable.

math.setup: Night prices: single $100, group $80, club $80 (night package $480/6 shows). Ticket mix: single 70%, group+club 30% (both priced at $80 for night). Per-show cost: $30,000.
math.answer: Thursday nights are unprofitable, losing approximately $1,800 per show. All other days are profitable. Sunday matinees are profitable but have a relatively slim margin.

questions.prompt: The client does not want to eliminate Thursday nights and believes the biggest opportunity is in club ticket sales. They want to allow customers to convert to a club membership after seeing one show as a single-ticket buyer. What percentage of Thursday single-ticket buyers would need to convert to a club membership to make Thursday break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate must first find the revenue gap to break even, then determine how many additional club tickets are needed at the club per-show price, then express that as a percentage of Thursday single-ticket buyers.

math.setup: Thursday revenue shortfall: $30,000 - $28,200 = $1,800. Club night package = $480/6 shows = $80 per show. Thursday single-ticket buyers = 70% of 300 = 210.
steps: Each converted club member contributes $80 per show (same as group price used in original calc)
Number of conversions needed = $1,800 / $80 = 22.5, approximately 23-25 tickets
Percentage of Thursday single-ticket buyers = 25 / 300 = ~8% (using round $2,000 shortfall) or 23/210 = ~11% of single-ticket buyers specifically
math.answer: Approximately 8-9% of Thursday night traffic (roughly 25 people out of 300) would need to convert to club memberships to reach break even. Expressed as a share of single-ticket buyers only (~210), the figure is roughly 11%.

brainstorming.prompt: What ideas would you suggest to raise club ticket sales or otherwise improve Thursday night profitability?

categories.name: Discounting / Pricing
ideas: Offer Thursday-specific discounts to boost volume
Bundle a Thursday ticket with a Saturday ticket at a combined discount
Retroactive club discount for first-time single-ticket buyers who convert

categories.name: Customer Acquisition
ideas: Target local residents who cannot travel on weekdays but can attend Thursday evening
Market to urban professionals as an after-work treat
Partner with corporations for group sales on Thursdays
Run referral programs for existing club members

categories.name: Club Membership Growth
ideas: Allow post-show club membership signup with retroactive discount
Offer trial memberships or introductory packages
Highlight club value proposition in pre-show and at-venue marketing

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Reduce variable staffing on low-attendance nights
Use only a portion of the theater on Thursdays to cut costs
Negotiate lower talent fees for weeknight performances

categories.name: Revenue Diversification
ideas: Expand concessions to increase per-customer spend
Add VIP seating tiers for premium pricing
Explore corporate sponsorships for Thursday performances

recommendation: The opera house is losing money on Thursday nights, primarily due to insufficient traffic (300 vs 500-seat capacity), which prevents covering the $30,000 per-show cost.
The most immediate lever is converting approximately 8-9% of Thursday single-ticket buyers to club memberships via a post-show signup program, which would return Thursday nights to break even.
Longer-term, the client should pursue a broader strategy to grow club membership and attract new customer segments to Thursday performances.
risks: Club conversion rate may fall short of the 8-9% target if the post-show experience does not sufficiently motivate signups
Discounting or bundling could erode overall revenue per customer if not carefully managed
Expanding the customer base beyond the traditional 45+ suburban demographic requires careful brand management to avoid alienating core patrons
next_steps: Pilot the post-show club membership conversion program and track conversion rates
Analyze demographic data to identify which customer segments are most receptive to Thursday attendance
Conduct a deeper cost analysis to identify whether any variable costs can be reduced on low-attendance nights
Explore concessions and premium seating as additional revenue streams
